title: Lesson 2: Close Read-aloud, Session 1: What Makes Day and Night
objective: Students will describe patterns of light and dark on earth using information from an informational text and record observations about the sun and moon using descriptive language.

what_is_taught.skill: describe patterns of light and dark on earth using information from a text
identify adjectives that describe the sun, moon, and stars
use adjectives to describe objects in pictures
record observations about the sun and moon using pictures and words
participate in oral discussions about text and observations
use sentence frames to formulate descriptive sentences
listen to and echo a poem with gestures and expression

student_actions.recognition_identification: listen to poem and text, identify adjectives and patterns
student_actions.oral_production: echo poem verses, discuss poem meaning and patterns, share observations orally
student_actions.written_production: participate in shared writing by contributing descriptive sentences and sketches
student_actions.reasoning_explanation: explain what the poem is about and what patterns are observed in the sky
student_actions.comprehension_response: answer questions about the poem and informational text, discuss learning target understanding and observations about day and night, describe adjectives found in poem verses and relate them to real objects, summarize learning target in own words

evidence.quote: Tell students that you will read the poem first on your own as they listen, then they should echo each verse as you read it a second time. Invite students to think of and use gestures and hand motions that go along with the poem as you read it aloud.
Read aloud the entire poem, slowly, fluently with expression, and without interruption.
After reading the final verse of the poem, invite students to turn and talk to an elbow partner: 'What is the poem about?' (what the sun, moon, and stars look like)
'What, in the poem, makes you think so?' (Responses will vary
Invite students to whisper a noun from the poem, 'What We See: The Sun, Moon, and Stars', into their hands. Then invite them to whisper a verb from the poem into their hands.

Tell students that this poem uses another kind of word as it describes what the sun, moon, and stars look like. Words that describe things like the sun, moon, and stars have a special name, adjectives. Define adjectives for students (words that describe a person, place, or thing).
'What words would you use to describe how the sun and moon look like in these photographs?' (The sun is yellow; the moon is round.)
What adjectives did you find in this verse?' (round and orange)
'What is something at home or at school that we could describe using this adjective?' (a basketball)
Circle and/or highlight the adjectives in each verse as you continue to read the poem aloud. Refer to 'What We See: The Sun, Moon, and Stars' poem (example, for teacher reference) as necessary.
Direct students' attention to the Unit 2 Guiding Question anchor chart and read the guiding question aloud:
'What is a pattern?' (something that happens over again)
'What have you noticed when you look at the sky?' (I see the sun and the moon.)
'What patterns have you noticed in these observations?' (I notice that the sun appears to

Share with students that today, they will begin reading a new book called What Makes Day and Night and will begin to collect information about different patterns that can be observed in the sky. Remind students that they will add this information to the Unit 2 Guiding Question anchor chart and will continue to add new information to the chart throughout the unit.

Guide students through the close read-aloud for What Makes Day and Night using the Close Read-aloud Guide: What Makes Day and Night (Session 1; for teacher reference). Consider using the Reading Informational Text Checklist during the close read-aloud (see Assessment Overview and Resources).

Refocus whole group. Give students specific, positive feedback on their close reading skills. (Example: 'I saw you listen to the text and study the illustrations to learn about how the earth rotates.')
I can describe the pattern of light and dark on earth using information from the text What Makes Day and Night.

Before beginning the close read-aloud, provide white boards and dry-erase markers as an option for students to record (in drawing or writing) their ideas. This will also help scaffold active listening for key details. (MMR, MMAE)
Refocus students whole group.

Tell students that today they will look at images of the sun and moon and then record their observations using pictures and words. Remind them that earlier in the lesson they identified adjectives, or words to describe something, to describe what the sun and moon look like.
Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group:
Display the Describing the Sun and Moon recording form and tell students that now they will use their ideas of what the sun and moon look like in a class shared writing activity.

As students share responses, use their ideas to complete page 1. Think aloud how to use the words from the question itself as a cue to formulate the answer using a complete sentence. (Example: The sun looks small and yellow.)
Draw a quick sketch of what the sun looks like.

As students share responses, use their ideas to complete page 2. Think aloud how to use the words from the question itself as a cue to formulate the answer using a complete sentence. (Example: The moon looks bright and white.)
Draw a quick sketch of what the moon looks like.
frame: 'The [sun/moon] looks like a(n) [adjective] [noun].' (Example: The sun looks like an orange ball. The sun looks bright and yellow.)
Refocus students whole group.
I can describe the pattern of light and dark on earth using information from the text What Makes Day and Night.
'How do our close read-aloud and shared writing add to your understanding of the pattern of light and dark on earth? I'll give you time to think and discuss with a partner.' (Responses will vary.)

'What have you learned about the pattern of light and dark on earth?' (Responses will vary, but may include: that day happens when the sun shines on our part of earth, and night happens when shadow covers our part of earth.)
Invite a few students to share out.

For ELLs: Check for comprehension by asking students to summarize and then to personalize the learning target. Ask them to paraphrase it and then to say how they feel about it. Example: 'Can you put the learning target in your own words?' (I can use what I learned from the text to tell about why we have night and day.) 'How do you feel about that target?' (I am excited to learn about it because I love the moon.)

teacher_actions.direct_instruction: Model reading the poem with expression and fluency; define nouns, verbs, and adjectives; model identifying adjectives in the poem; model reading the guiding question and explaining the concept of patterns; model close read-aloud of informational text; model shared writing using descriptive sentences and sketches; model reflection and summarizing learning targets.

scope.breadth: introduce and explore patterns in the sky, descriptive language, and observational recording
scope.depth: close reading of informational text, identifying adjectives, shared writing with descriptive sentences

context.stimulus_provided: informational text What Makes Day and Night, poem 'What We See: The Sun, Moon, and Stars', photographs of sun and moon, recording forms

sections_covered.warm_up: Engaging the Learner: 'What We See: The Sun, Moon, and Stars' Poem
sections_covered.direct_instruction: Structured Discussion: Introducing the Unit 2 Guiding Question
sections_covered.guided_practice: Close Read-aloud, Session 1: What Makes Day and Night, Pages 1-31
sections_covered.independent_application: Shared Writing: Describing the Sun and Moon

supports.english_language_learners: Supports include sentence frames, partner pairing with more proficient speakers, picture cues, and word walls with picture cards.
supports.universal_design_udl: Options for recording ideas using drawing or writing; total participation techniques; use of gestures and hand motions during poem reading.
supports.below_level_reinforce: Use of picture cues and word walls to support expressive language.
supports.above_level_extend: Encourage students to provide evidence and explain their thinking during discussions.

assessment.method: oral responses during discussions, shared writing contributions, and comprehension checks

text_complexity.qualitative: informational text with illustrations; moderate language and knowledge demands
text_complexity.reader_and_task: text read aloud to reduce decoding load; students engage in listening, discussion, and shared writing tasks
